title: Why Norris’ ‘masterpiece’ Madrid pole lap was ‘almost unrepeatable’
excerpt:
A quite remarkable lap from Lando Norris at the end of Q3 in Madrid secured a third pole position in four races for the McLaren driver, and prompted his team boss Andrea Stella to describe it as a “bit of a masterpiece”.

This one was special not just in the context of the 2026 season, but also the whole of Norris' career.

Perhaps the most remarkable thing was that a slide at the 22nd and final corner, as his tyres began to cry enough, cost him over 0.3 sec – and yet he was already so far up on where he’d been before that it was still good enough to secure his 19th career pole.

It was a performance that was enjoyed as much by the McLaren pit wall as by watching fans, especially as it appeared to come out of the blue.

“I would say that definitely this was one of the most impressive laps that I witnessed, as somebody that watches telemetry in 450 Grands Prix,” said Stella afterwards.

“Because we were not honestly performing to the level of scoring of pole position. I think at no stage during the weekend we demonstrated that the car was performing at the level of being the best car.

“We were lacking quite significantly in the first sector – low-speed and kerbing – and for the drivers it was a very difficult car to nail a lap. We saw that there were spells of potential, but it's always very difficult to put it together.”

As Stella noted, the pole lap would have been more notable without the loss of time at the end of it.

“I think the most impressive thing is the fact that it's a pole position despite having lost three and a half tenths in the last corner,” said the Italian. “Which means that it would have been a pretty convincing pole position without this issue.

“At the same time, this issue is a consequence of pushing to the level that Lando managed to push. But today, everyone will push the limits.

"The thing that makes the lap unique, when you look especially at the telemetry, is the precision, the braking, the speed you carry an entry, the striking of the kerb, the going on power – everything is executed with a pretty unique level of precision.

“So for me, that's if anything the main attribute that would associate to this lap, just the incredible precision in the metre-by-metre execution.”

Through the weekend the McLaren engineering team focussed on that critical first part of the lap, with its pair of tight complexes at Turns 1 and 2, and 5, 5A and 6.

Progress wasn’t helped by the gearbox issue that cost Norris crucial track time in FP2, but into FP3 and Qualifying further tweaks gradually brought the improvements that the team were seeking.

“Shout out to Lando, but let me say also to the team,” said Stella. “Because we had the clear objective from the first runs in practice to add some low-speed performance and kerbing performance.

“And we kept doing that session after session, but obviously P2 was a bit of loss of ground, because Lando lost pretty much the entire session. So I think this makes his work in Qualifying even more remarkable. And also on Oscar, we were experiencing a little problem on the car, so we didn't have great references. We kept learning, we kept putting this together.”

Stella stressed that the challenge was to overcome the inherent characteristics of the MCL40.

“The car much more naturally performs well in high-speed, fast-flowing sections,” he said. “But struggles to be consistent when you brake and you carry the brakes into low-speed, and then you have to hit a kerb – it's very unpredictable.

“And here there's many of these kinds of corners. So to start with, in FP1, we saw the difficulties. What I appreciated in the work of the team is that we gave ourselves a clear objective, and we started to nail several areas of the setup that ultimately compounded and allowed the performance of the car to go to another level.

“So corner 5, corner 6, I think it's one of the most difficult corners of the entire championship. The fact that a McLaren could have the fastest Sector 1, it was not only in 5 and 6, we can see in the GPS overlays that we are also the fastest in corner 1 and 2.

“But once again, the amount of kerb that you take in corner 1 and landing without upsetting the car, this is why I say the lap was almost unrepeatable, because all this was nailed. So the gain in Sector 1 comes 50% in 5/6, but the other 50% in corner 1 and 2.”

The set-up tweaks also paid off as Stella further explained: “Like I said before, the car was completely changed from the start of FP1 to perform well in these two corners, and corner 7 and corner 20. These are the places where we focussed, because we knew that in the other corners the performance was coming quite naturally for the characteristics of the car.

“And in these places, we forced the car to work, but still the performance needed to be extracted. And like I said, this required a level of precision that thankfully we were able to deploy in the final run of Q3. But you know, that lap gives you a sense that it would be difficult to be repeated.”

He added: “Still, I think the exploitation of car potential for the pole position lap is pretty unique. I would say that if we put another set of tyres, I mean, we would gain three-tenths in the last corner, but I'm not sure we would be able to repeat what Lando was able to do in the first 21 corners.”

The only downside for Norris and the team was that slide at the very end of the lap as the tyres were past their best.

“I think in the last corner he just paid the price of the fact that the lap was coming like one second faster than any other lap,” Stella explained.

“Therefore, there was quite a lot more that was extracted from the tyres. But the tyres were tired, and somehow Lando did not take this into account, and he entered the corner with the same impetus that he had in some other corners.

“I think it's just a little bit of a toll that was presented by the tyres – he oversteered in entry, and this means that he loses completely the racing line. And like I say, he lost more than three-tenths.”

title: What the teams said – Qualifying in Spain
excerpt:
McLaren

Lando Norris did not look rusty despite siting out FP2, winding up right in the mix in final practice along with his team mate. As such, hopes were high of a strong showing come Qualifying. Oscar Piastri had to use a second set of softs to make it out of Q2, the team exercising caution even though he would have made it anyway.

That left him with only one run on new rubber in Q3, and the Australian failed to execute his lap and was disparaging about his efforts afterwards. But Norris absolutely nailed his final run with a lap he described as one of his very best, the McLaren man grabbing his third pole of the season by the narrowest of margins.

Lando Norris, 1st, 1:31.824

"I'm incredibly proud of that lap. It was one of those moments where everything clicks and you're able to extract exactly what you set out to achieve. The car felt strong, I felt confident, and that final lap was as close to perfect as I've managed around this circuit. To secure Pole position for the first Formula 1 race at the Madring makes it even more special. A big thank you to the team for all their hard work. We've put ourselves in the best possible position for tomorrow and now the focus is on converting that into a strong result on race day."

Oscar Piastri, 7th, 1:32.294

“P7. I’m a bit disappointed with that one. Overall, it was a bit of a messy session and the car felt nicer in FP3 than it did in Qualifying. We improved it a bit through the three Quali sessions, but I didn’t have that last bit we needed in the last run. The first lap of Q3 on used tyres was okay, but my final run on new tyres wasn’t good enough. Around this track, once you’re out of rhythm it’s very hard to get it back, and needing two sets in Q1 put on the back foot a bit.

“The positives are that the car is fast and Lando’s Pole shows what’s possible when you hook it up. For tomorrow, tyre degradation is a bit of a question mark after the graining we saw in practice, and overtaking won’t be straightforward, so it’ll come down to strategy and staying out of trouble. We’ll review everything as a team tonight, keep it clean, and try to make the most of our pace in the race.”

Andrea Stella, Team Principal

“Today's Pole position is a masterpiece from Lando and a fantastic reward for the entire team's hard work. We knew the potential was in the car, but we had to work diligently all weekend to unlock our performance in the low-speed corners. Lando's lap was at the level of a World Champion, and the most incredible part is that he secured Pole despite a three-tenth mistake in the final corner, which shows just how much pace we truly had. It's a testament to his talent, especially after missing a practice session, and to the brilliant work from everyone at the track and back at the factory to give him that confidence.

"While we are thrilled with Pole, we are not entirely satisfied as we feel there was more to be achieved with Oscar, who was unfortunately just a fraction away from a much higher grid slot in this incredibly tight field. Looking to the race, there are many unknowns for everyone. We have very limited data on high fuel and tyre behaviour, which will make for an uncertain and entertaining race for the fans. Starting from the best possible position is a huge advantage, but we know we will have to master all the variables tomorrow to convert this into a strong result."

Mercedes

When Kimi Antonelli topped the disrupted FP3 session for Mercedes, the youngster looked favourite for pole. He was quick from word go in Qualifying too, and grabbed provisional pole with his last run in Q3, only to be beaten by 0.011s as Norris just snatched it. Still, second is a great starting slot at a track where overtaking might be tricky.

George Russell looked to be right there with his team mate, fastest in Q1, and matching the Italian in the first sector on his last flying run of Q3. But his lap tailed away and with such a tightly packed field, he wound up just sixth with some very fast cars between himself and his team mate – and Championship rival - tomorrow.

Kimi Antonelli, 2nd, 1:31.835

"I put together a strong lap on my final effort, and I thought it might have been good enough for pole position. Credit to Lando (Norris) though. He and McLaren did a great job and managed to snatch it away right at the last.

"It was a very intense qualifying session where it was difficult to get the balance right with the tyres with the track being so hot. It was difficult to get the out-lap preparation right but then to also make sure you had it in the right window for all of your push lap. Overall, I think we did a good job and can be pleased with our efforts.

"Tomorrow will be a big challenge for everyone with lots of unknowns. Whilst overtaking will be tough, I hope we can put Lando under pressure and see what we can do to fight for victory. Managing the tyres will be key so let’s see what we can do."

George Russell, 6th, 1:32.149

"It was a tough qualifying session for me today. The main factor we were managing throughout all the sessions was ensuring we had the tyres in the right window. I had a really good lap in Q1 and hoped that I had the same potential in my last lap of Q3. Unfortunately, it was a bit of a scrappy lap; I had a lot of understeer from turn 11 onwards and lost a couple of tenths from there. The tyres really struggle here with the heat and the long corners, so you can find yourself sliding around, losing more time, and being pushed further down the order.

"Understanding the tyres more ahead of tomorrow will be crucial as while it didn’t all come together for me today, I hope tomorrow I’ll be able to make my way through the pack. We saw high tyre degradation on Friday and if that repeats itself tomorrow, then there will definitely be opportunities for us to make good progress."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"Coming into the weekend, we didn’t expect to be in the fight for pole. As we moved towards qualifying though we had shown good pace and thought that we may have an opportunity to get P1. We came close but in the final moments, Lando (Norris) pulled out the lap of the weekend so far. Credit to him and McLaren for that; we are still relatively satisfied with our performance though as it gives us a chance to battle at the front tomorrow.

"On George’s side, he never felt completely comfortable with the car. We were trying to add more front-wing as qualifying progressed to give him more confidence but that is not the best position to be in as a driver, particularly on a circuit where you want to be hammering in the laps and getting used to the car. That said, it was very close out there and the margins at the front were very small.

"Overtaking will be tough tomorrow. It has not looked easy in any of the junior formula races but hopefully we get some good action tomorrow. There are several unknowns that could make for an interesting race too."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We expected this weekend to be more challenging than Monza, not because the car doesn't suit the circuit necessarily, but because this is a track that rewards downforce and we've gone nearly four months without introducing a major update. Even so, our pace through practice was encouraging and, heading into qualifying, we felt we were firmly in the fight for pole position.

"Traffic management was particularly difficult in the early stages because a competitive lap here relies on having a clean out lap. Once we came through Q1, though, we were able to build some rhythm and both drivers continued to find time as track grip improved.

"Kimi put together a strong final lap but ultimately fell just short of matching Lando (Norris). George also improved on his last run but suffered front washout in Turn 11 and then experienced higher tyre temperatures through the remainder of the lap, which cost him grip and lap time.

"Making progress tomorrow will not be straightforward as overtaking looks very difficult. However, if the tyre degradation we saw earlier in the weekend remains a factor, it could create opportunities for us to be creative with strategy and put ourselves in the fight."

Red Bull

Liam Lawson was just the third driver of the weekend to sample the hard tyre in practice, but he did not get many laps on the C2 rubber before the red flags came out. Between that, and Max Verstappen coming out late in FP3, Red Bull’s form heading into Qualifying had a question mark. But both drivers made it to Q3 with ease in a solid showing.

Once there, Lawson’s first lap did not go to plan and in the end, he had to settle for eighth. Verstappen nailed his last run to beat both Ferrari cars, something that not many would have guessed yesterday. Starting P3, the Dutchman could well be challenging for his second podium in a row.

Max Verstappen, 3rd, 1:31.964

“It was a very strong Qualifying from our side, and a top-three result is something we can be quite happy with. We made some nice improvements to the setup and got the car into a good window. From Q1 through to Q3, we were able to build with each run and stay competitive at the front throughout.

"We ended up pretty close to Pole and only really lost out in the final sector, but we'll see what we can do from the second row tomorrow. From the practice sessions, we know that tyre life is going to be crucial and something we need to stay on top of if we want to fight with our rivals.

"Overtaking opportunities are hard to come by here and passing won't be easy, so getting the strategy right will be important. If we do that, I think we have a good car for the race.”

Liam Lawson, 8th, 1:32.316

“We looked competitive at the start of Qualifying, so it would have been nice to be fighting a little further up the order, but unfortunately Q3 did not quite come together for us. As the session progressed, everyone around us seemed to find a bit more lap time, whereas we were not able to make the same step.

"I am happy with the progress we have made compared to where we were earlier in the week, and I am feeling more comfortable in the car every time I get behind the wheel. There are still a few things for us to learn and take into tomorrow, but overall it has been a positive step forward.

"It is a difficult track to overtake on and a place where pushing the limits is always a challenge, so making up positions will not be easy unless opportunities come our way. The car has looked quick all weekend, though, and I am excited for the race. Hopefully we can put ourselves in the mix and move forward tomorrow.”

Laurent Mekies, Team Principal

"A really strong result for the whole Team today on such a challenging track, especially with the gaps at the front being so incredibly tight. Max was at the top of his game as always. He was competitive throughout Qualifying, fastest in Q2 by just a few hundredths and right in the fight for pole until the very last moment. Naturally, there is some disappointment when you miss out on the front row by such a small margin, but Max delivered another exceptional performance and it was also very encouraging to see Liam right in the mix, only a few tenths away.

"This is an extremely demanding circuit, with a combination of low-speed and high-speed corners, aggressive kerbs and walls that leave very little room for error. To see both drivers able to push with confidence in these conditions is a good indication of the progress with the underlying pace of the car and a deserved reward for all the hard work from everyone back in Milton Keynes.

"Tomorrow presents a different challenge. The gap between the top four teams is extremely small, so hopefully we can be right in the fight once again. Strategy will play an important role, particularly depending on how difficult overtaking proves to be, and we will need to stay flexible in what could be an unpredictable race. With two cars in the mix and every opportunity to be in the podium fight, we are looking forward to seeing what we can achieve tomorrow."

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton was the first to bring out the red flags in final practice, after locking up and running straight into the barriers. Despite a broken front wing, he initially tried to bring the car home before being told to stop by the team. That cost him some track time, but it did not seem to hamper the Ferrari man come Qualifying.

He was right in the mix from word go, trading fast laps with team mate Charles Leclerc. Both made it through Q1 on the mediums, meaning they have a set of new softs for tomorrow if needed. In Q3, Hamilton grabbed provisional pole on the first runs, but was beaten by less than two tenths on the second runs. He did pip his team mate though, Leclerc just .006s further back in fifth.

Lewis Hamilton, 4th, 1:32.013

"Although the session didn’t quite end with the result we wanted, it was a solid performance overall. The car felt good throughout. My first lap in Q3 was strong, but it didn’t quite come together on the final run, which cost us a few positions.

"P4 isn’t where I think we could have been, but there are positives to take from the session. It’s a great circuit to drive, and tomorrow will be about consistency and tyre management. Degradation could be a key factor, so the focus will be on executing well and making the most of every opportunity in the race."

Charles Leclerc, 5th, 1:32.019

"It’s an interesting track to drive on. There may have been a bit of margin for extracting more, but all in all, it was quite a good lap. There aren’t many spots where overtaking is possible here, so we will see how the race unfolds and try to take any opportunity we have to get ahead."

Fred Vasseur, Team Principal

"When you are P1 after the first run in Q3, for sure you are targeting pole. I think Lewis made a small mistake at the start of his last flying lap and left around a tenth and a half in the first sector. Charles did a good lap and improved massively through Turns 5 and 6, but with such small gaps between the cars, it was not enough to do better than fifth.

"Now let’s focus on tomorrow: the data from long runs on Friday might not be fully representative, as no one really focused on this and the track is still evolving very quickly. From today’s F2 and F3 races, it’s clear that overtaking is extremely difficult on this track but we also know the race could be chaotic, so we need to be ready to take every opportunity, whether that comes from a VSC, a Safety Car or even a red flag."

Alpine

It was a mixed bag for Alpine in Qualifying, with both drivers leaving it late to set a lap time in Q2 after their initial runs were interrupted by yellow flags. Franco Colapinto had already had a hairy moment, just catching his car through La Monumental in a very impressive show of skill. He nailed his last run with the pressure on to make Q3, and grabbed ninth on the grid.

Pierre Gasly overcooked his run in Q2, hitting the wall which cost him and he exited at the second time of asking.

Pierre Gasly, 14th, 1:33.753

“We have a lot to work on and understand after today's result. I was optimistic going into Qualifying as the car felt good all the way through Practice and the pace felt like it was definitely there for the top ten. I just seemed to struggle with grip and the car was sliding around quite a lot and really a handful to drive. It feels like something is not right and I am sure the team and I will sit down and really try to understand why we were too slow in Qualifying. It is not over yet, though, and our aim is always to come away from races with points. We know it will be a challenging race starting from P14 but our pace in Free Practice 2 on high fuel was promising so we have every reason to be confident for tomorrow. We are not sure what the racing will be like at this circuit, it will likely be very tough, but I will give it my all to recover back up into the top ten.”

Franco Colapinto, 9th, 1:32.903

“I am very proud to be in Q3 today. Yesterday was tricky, I did not feel 100% in the car and we have had to work hard as a team to find improvements and build up our confidence all the way up to Qualifying. In the end, I did some of my best laps and that is good enough for P9 on the grid for tomorrow's race. It's definitely a difficult track and we know it does not suit our package too well, so we have really had to take things step by step. I was still learning a lot during Qualifying and we performed very well and I think we maximised everything. I did have a moment at Turn 12, it was very fast and I had to correct it. Tomorrow might be tricky for overtaking and we really do not know what might happen at this track. It might be quite limited on chances so our focus will be on maximising everything we can control and, of course, aiming for points at the end of the race.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“It was an exciting Qualifying session at a new track, and you could see all the drivers pushing on the limit. That's what Formula One is all about and is testament to the skill on show today. Heading into Qualifying, we were trying to get the drivers into a comfortable place with the car, and have it behave and handle the way they need it. We knew we were in a fight to get into Q3 and it would be close with Racing Bulls and Audi. Franco did a brilliant job and looking at the times, ninth place ahead of Arvid [Lindblad] was probably the best outcome. On Pierre's side, he expressed that he wasn't happy with the car, so we need to understand why that was the case and what we can do to help him for tomorrow's race. We've seen from other races and support series here, this layout can throw up a few unknowns and it could be a race of attrition tomorrow. So, we need to stay focused and be there at the end to score as many points as we can.”

Audi

Audi were the only team to run the mediums in FP3, although they did not get many laps in thanks to the red flags. On the softs both drivers finished in the top 10, so the team had decent hopes of a strong Qualifying, but they were just pipped in the end and had to settle for P11 and P12.

Nico Hulkenberg beat his team mate by just over a tenth, but they will need better starts than they managed in Monza if they want to fight forward and bag points for the fifth time in the last six Grands Prix.

Nico Hulkenberg, 11th, 1:33.223

"It was incredibly tight today, and we missed out on Q3 by just 0.019s. We knew qualifying around a brand-new circuit would be close, and that's exactly how it turned out. Tomorrow is still a bit of an unknown. It's the first race here, so nobody really knows how things will unfold. We have to be ready for whatever comes our way. The priority will be to stay out of trouble early on, and then see what we can make of the race."

Gabriel Bortoleto, 12th, 1:33.388

“I actually think today was not too bad, but it was difficult to put the perfect lap together. In all fairness, it's been a bit of an odd weekend so far: we have changed the car quite a lot from yesterday, and I did find more confidence in Qualifying, but I think there was definitely more on the table for us today.

“Looking at tomorrow, I think there is a chance for us to move forward, but it will depend a lot on our pace and how much tyre degradation will impact us. As always, we’ll give our best and see where it takes us.”

Allan McNish, Racing Director

"It was a very tight qualifying session at a circuit on which getting laps together is not easy. Despite this, both Nico and Gabi, as well as the crews, were able to deliver a good performance. Unfortunately, less than two hundredths of a second was the difference between getting into Q3 or not for Nico: it was a tiny margin, but we were just on the wrong side of that. I think that was the most we could extract for our car, so we can't be too disappointed with that. Overall, with both cars up there on the edge of the top ten, it was another strong performance by the team, especially in light of the upgrades our rivals have brought in the last few races."

Haas

Ollie Bearman lost the rear and spun into the barriers late in FP3, walking away from what looked a decent hit. Unfortunately, that ended his involvement for the day with too much car damage for the team to repair in time for Qualifying. Considering their upgrades have looked to move them up the order here, it was a double blow for the team.

Esteban Ocon made Q3 with relative ease, grabbing 13th on the grid. That is his best Qualifying performance since Japan, showing just how much improvement the team have managed to find through those aero upgrades.

Oliver Bearman, 21st, No time set in Q1

“It’s a shame as the car was quick. It was a tough day yesterday, but we made some changes overnight, and the car was feeling really good in FP3. Unfortunately, I got caught out in Turn 10 on the final lap, and it was a combination of the tyres being a bit old and I had a gust of wind not in my favor. I shouldn’t have made that mistake – it hurts a lot as the car was strong, but I’m sure there can be some opportunities tomorrow. We have to dust ourselves off and look at the positives, which is that the car was fast and we’ll be giving it everything to do the best we can tomorrow.”

Esteban Ocon, 13th, 1:33.667

“I’m firstly happy that Ollie is okay, that was a big one. After that, we went into Quali with a much better feeling this weekend. We easily got into Q2 for a fourth time in a row, which is very positive, and that last lap was pretty well maximised, I’m pretty happy with it. We were still quite far from the Audis, so we need to look into that, but so far it’s a much better weekend than Monza, where the car is healthy, working how it should, and we need to keep pushing to see if we can get more out of tomorrow. We weren’t in Q3, so we have a set of new tyres over those in front, and I have a feeling it could be quite an entertaining race.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“In FP3, we were very happy with the car, the drivers were happy and performing, and we looked competitive. It’s unfortunate that Ollie shunted at the end of FP3, but he’s a great driver and a great guy, and the reason we’re still P7 in the Constructors’ Championship is because in some races, he really delivered. I have no doubt that will happen again, it’s just sadly happened in a weekend where we have a competitive car – but it happens, it’s racing. We had severe damage and couldn’t get the car ready for Qualifying.

“Esteban’s been having a really good weekend, making progress at a very difficult circuit. His performance in Qualifying was solid, and the fact that it was much hotter in Qualifying, I think we went backwards compared to FP3, but I think it’s pretty obvious why, so that’s something we’re aware of to improve later in the season. Esteban did a good job getting P13, it’s a decent place to start, right behind our direct competitors, so we’ll see what we can do tomorrow from there.”

Williams

Carlos Sainz had a moment in FP3, locking up and running straight on, just avoiding the barriers. But Alex Albon was not so fortunate, as he clipped the walls with his rear tyre and broke a track rod, ending his session early.

As such, the Thai driver was up against it in Q1 but pulled a late lap out to scrape into Q2, much to his delight. Sainz could not join him, the Spaniard exiting at the first time of asking in a disappointing afternoon at his home race.

His day later got worse, as Sainz was handed a three-place grid drop for impeding Bottas in Q1 and thus will start from P20.

Carlos Sainz, 17th, 1:35.312

“It was a good lap but a scrappy qualifying overall, with several issues that cost us precious tenths in the end. We knew we would struggle at this track but we also went out very early for the last push, losing out on track evolution, and had some deployment losses that prevented us from getting into Q2. Apologies to Valtteri for impeding his lap, I wasn’t aware he was pushing and had no time to get out of his way.

On a positive note, this track has been a lot of fun to drive at qualifying pace, and I’m enjoying being so close to the walls and always driving at the limit. It’s been incredible to feel the support of the fans throughout the weekend so far, and it’s a dream come true to be here racing in front of my home crowd. Tomorrow, overtaking will be difficult, but we will try our best to come back and give everyone something to cheer for!”

Alex Albon, 16th, 1:35.532

“I’m happy to be through to Q2 today after what’s been a tough weekend so far. I was on the back foot going into this session, having only done a handful of laps, especially at a track like Madrid where you need a lot of laps to get up to speed. We changed some parts on the car, which thankfully paid off and got us out of Q1, which is an achievement given all the issues we’ve faced. Tomorrow will be a challenge as it’s not an overtaking track, but we’ll do what we can to get a good result.”

James Vowles, Team Principal

“It's been fantastic to be in Madrid - really impressed with the track, the facilities, the environment. It is really world class. It was always predicted to be a tough weekend for us and unfortunately that's transpiring to be the case. Well done to Alex, he had almost no laps underneath his belt after a small incident in FP3 but put in a really strong lap to put that car into Q2.

“With Carlos, as you saw there was just milliseconds between the two drivers as there always is. The impeding penalty is the team's responsibility - we didn't warn Carlos of Valtteri behind him and we need to change and improve our systems to make sure we do so in future. We are not here to be fighting for 17th but we will give our all tomorrow. It is a race that I feel could present some twists and turns and we need to be ready for them when they come.”

Aston Martin

Aston Martin broke curfew after detecting an issue with Lance Stroll’s battery pack, and the team opted to change some of his PU components, meaning a grid drop for Sunday. A further issue was detected in Q1, and the Canadian did not come back out to set a lap time – with the team saying a suspected water pressure issue was the cause. Fernando Alonso did compete, but could not extract enough pace from the car to make Q2.

Fernando Alonso, 18th, 1:35.388

“The circuit was challenging and it’s a high adrenaline lap at high speeds. I think it was probably the maximum we could achieve today in Qualifying and we’ll have to see what we can do in the race. It looks like overtaking might be difficult, so we’ll have to try to maximise everything to gain positions. The fans were very enthusiastic today and it is great to see so much green and energy from the grandstands.”

Lance Stroll, 22nd, No time set in Q1

“We had a water pressure issue in Qualifying. We knew we’d be starting at the back of the grid anyway with the components we replaced overnight, but I was looking forward to getting some more laps in around here. It’s clear we still have a lot to work on. There could be some opportunities tomorrow though, so we’ll just run our own race and see how it goes.”

Cadillac

Cadillac had a solid day in terms of reliability, with both cars completing plenty of laps. Come Qualifying, they did not have the pace to fight with Williams in the end and had to settle for an intra-team battle. That was won by Sergio Perez, with Valtteri Bottas unable to set a representative lap time in the end after being impeded by Sainz. That ended a run of five Qualifying sessions where the Finnish racer has been on top.

Sergio Perez, 19th, 1:35.913

“It's an amazing track and I’m really happy to be here. The atmosphere is incredible and I'm very happy with my qualifying lap. We were very aggressive with our program. I have to say a well done to the team. We maximised our package and further closed the gap to the Williams and Aston Martin teams ahead. Although it was not enough to progress into Q2, it was a really strong lap. The team has also been strong operationally, so I’m very satisfied with that. Tomorrow should present some opportunities to us, so we need to make sure we continue executing as we have been so far this weekend and I’m sure we can have a good race.”

Valtteri Bottas, 20th, 1:38.011

“It’s been a tricky weekend for us. You always want to get the most out of the car and today we couldn’t quite get there. We know that we’re lacking in the high speed corners, and it’s a tough track as there are so many blind spots. I was the first car out in the beginning, but after that was compromised by traffic which was unlucky but sometimes that’s how it goes. We’ll go again tomorrow in the race and hopefully there will be some opportunities.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“Madring is a great addition to the Formula 1 calendar and a big challenge for the drivers. Overall, it was a reasonable qualifying performance today. Checo did well to get the most out of the car. Valtteri struggled to adjust to the lower grip during the session and was improving although it is a shame that he was clearly impeded on his flying lap.

“We are expecting that tomorrow will be a tough, hot and demanding race. It is a track which will test the tyres and concentration. It will be important to stay out of trouble, execute cleanly and make the most of every opportunity.”

Pirelli

Dario Marrafuschi, Pirelli Motorsport Director

"Today’s sessions confirmed the strong performance level of the Soft compound. Despite the free practice sessions being affected by a lengthy interruption, the teams were able to evaluate different ways of using the C4, with some drivers managing to improve their lap times even within the same run, thanks to track evolution and increasing confidence with the circuit. For some drivers, a slight drop in performance was observed in the final sector, mainly due to overheating, but overall the red-marked tyre worked extremely well. In fact, compared to the simulations, the quickest qualifying times were around half a second faster.

"It was also interesting to see some teams choose to tackle Q1 on the Medium compound, thereby preserving a fresh set of Soft tyres for the race. The performance gap between the two compounds is clear, but not significant enough to prevent those with sufficient pace margin from progressing without immediately resorting to the softer option.

"The picture for Sunday remains very open. A one-stop strategy currently appears to be the most natural choice, given the difficulty of overtaking and the time lost in the pit lane. However, a two-stop strategy could still prove competitive if degradation remains at the levels observed on Friday.

"The most likely strategies revolve around the Medium-Hard and Medium-Hard-Hard combinations. The Soft-Hard and Soft-Hard-Hard alternatives are estimated to be around two seconds slower over race distance. The C2 is undoubtedly the most consistent compound, and the majority of drivers have preserved both sets for precisely that reason.

"Much will depend, however, on the possible deployment of the Safety Car or Virtual Safety Car, a scenario which, on a street circuit with barriers so close to the track, represents, as we have already seen during the previous sessions, a factor that must be taken very seriously."

title: Russell explains how tyre troubles ruined pole chance in Madrid
excerpt:
George Russell has identified overheating tyres as the main reason his pace dropped off in Qualifying at the Madring, where he fell out of pole position contention and wound up P6.

The Briton appeared to get to grips with the new circuit faster than most as he topped the times in the opening practice hour, but he lost out to his competitors as the sessions went on and placed P5 and P6 in FP2 and FP3 respectively.

He nevertheless recovered some performance heading into the all-important Qualifying, setting the fastest lap in Q1 despite sharing concerns after he brushed the wall on his first effort.

While the top-10 shootout offered Russell the chance to claim his fifth pole of the season, he was unable to match the likes of Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli and ultimately wound up sixth – his lowest Qualifying result since the Hungarian Grand Prix.

“I was in the mix to fight for pole and on that last lap of Q3, I just really pushed the limit,” he reflected. “I was about three tenths up and then lost it all towards the end of the lap with the tyres overheating.

“That was quite a shame. It was really close between everyone out there and here we are.”

Russell previously delivered a frank verdict of his title chances heading into this weekend, accepting that Antonelli had “done a better job” across the season to date and deserves his current lead of 66 points in the Drivers’ Championship.

Although anything could happen in Sunday’s Spanish Grand Prix, Russell acknowledged that his continued tyre issues will hold him back unless Mercedes can find a solution overnight.

He added: “I jumped in the car and felt very comfortable here, and confident. As the track has got faster, I’ve been struggling to get the most out of the tyres.

“I’ve just been sliding rather than going round the corners faster, and I need to understand why that is.”

title: Verstappen explains focus for Spanish GP from P3
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has set out the areas that Red Bull will be focusing on during Sunday’s Spanish Grand Prix, with the Dutchman left feeling positive about his P3 result in Qualifying.

Verstappen had finished no higher than fifth across all three practice sessions held at the Madring circuit, having admitted at the end of Friday that he and the team were still “getting up to speed” with each lap.

The four-time World Champion went fastest during Q2 of Qualifying, however, and later secured third place in Q3, beaten only by polesitter Lando Norris and championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Quizzed on how he felt about the result afterwards – and if it was better than he had expected – Verstappen responded: “Yeah, the car was honestly in a quite decent window, and for us I think to be in the top three in Qualifying is good. We can be happy with that.

“I think still there's room for improvement – there can be some improvements made, especially in the final sector.

“That's where we really were struggling probably a little bit too much with our deployment strategy. So that's things to learn for in the future, but for us to be in the top three is good.”

Looking ahead to Sunday’s Grand Prix – the first Formula 1 race to be held at the Madring – Verstappen explained that tyre management will be a key focus for the event.

“[It could be] a long race, tough on tyres, so we'll be really about managing that and trying to really extract the most out of it and see what we can do,” the 28-year-old said.

title: Antonelli rues pole slipping away in ‘intense’ Qualifying
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has admitted that he was pleased with his effort in Spanish Grand Prix Qualifying before McLaren’s Lando Norris pipped him to pole position, with the Mercedes driver concluding that it was a “very intense” session at the Madring.

Fresh from his historic victory at the Italian Grand Prix, it looked as though Antonelli would be in front once again as he mingled around the top of the timesheets throughout Qualifying and consistently improved his laps.

His last lap in Q3 was enough to deny Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton pole, but in the final seconds, Norris completed what he labelled “one of the best laps” of his career to snatch P1 by margin of 0.011s over the 20-year-old.

Speaking straight afterwards, Antonelli said of his attempt: “I thought it was a good lap, but then this guy just snatched it away, so a good job to them.

“On my side, a very intense Qualifying – difficult to get the balance right with the track being so hot, but yeah, the lap was pretty clean.

“Obviously it's not easy to put the things together on a track like this, which is quite tricky, but overall I think we did a good job and now we'll try to see what we can do tomorrow.”

The Italian will be hoping to find a way past Norris and add an eighth win to his tally in the Spanish Grand Prix, but many teams have predicted that overtaking will be a significant challenge due to the circuit’s complex layout and lack of long straights.

A strong result would provide a further boost to Antonelli’s title ambitions – he currently holds a 66-point advantage over his nearest rival and team mate George Russell, who could only manage P6 in Qualifying.

Asked what his plan is for the race, Antonelli replied: “Hopefully a good start. Hopefully we can get the jump. If the opportunity comes to win the race, we’ll try to take it.

“Otherwise, we’ll just try to do our best race and then we’ll see what happens.”

title: Sainz hit with grid penalty for Spanish GP
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has been handed a grid penalty for the Spanish Grand Prix after a Qualifying infringement.

The Williams driver was found to have impeded Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac during Saturday's Qualifying session through Turn 7 in the final minutes of Q1.

Sainz initially qualified P17 for Sunday's 57-lap race, the first to be held at the Madring, while Bottas was left in P20 as neither progressed through to the second part of Qualifying.

The stewards heard from both Sainz and Bottas post-session, as well as looking at on-board videos and data before making their decision.

They noted that: "The team failed to inform the driver of Car 55 about Car 77 closing in on a flying lap and the driver did not take any action to make way for the incoming car.

It added: "The Stewards determine that Car 55 unnecessarily impeded Car 77", and handed Sainz a penalty for his home race.

"Not a very clean session, two or three issues that cost us probably there at the end, five-milliseconds to get through to Q2," said Sainz before the post-Qualifying penalty.

"A combination of just lacking a bit of performance on the straights. After looking at that lap, a couple of tenths.

"Then going very early for the last run and also impeding Valtteri, I just heard we impeded him without any notice from the pit wall.

"Not our cleanest session. Still did a pretty good lap but unfortunately not enough to make it through to Q2."

title: Hamilton reflects on missing pole for Spanish GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes himself and Ferrari have "got to work harder" in order to increase performance, having missed out on pole position for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix.

The Briton headed into Qualifying on the back foot after crashing head-on into the barrier at the final corner in Free Practice 3, eventually stopping his damaged car after calls from the team to pull over on the way back to the pits.

The missed track time earlier on Saturday didn't seem to hamper the seven-time World Champion, though, and Hamilton sat on provisional pole position after the first flying laps in the pivotal Q3 session.

But Hamilton slipped down to fourth in the final reckoning despite improving his time and finishing less than two tenths behind polesitter, Lando Norris.

"The only thing to say about FP3 is nothing. Qualifying was pretty decent," said Hamilton when asked to reflect on his day.

"Generally been feeling pretty decent. It takes everything for us to be able to compete with the two powerhouse motors [Mercedes and McLaren] ahead.

"They just seem to be able to turn the engine up or something when we get to Qualifying which we can't match. We've got to work harder."

Ferrari team mate Charles Leclerc finished directly behind Hamilton and was also within two tenths of Norris' top time, with the Monegasque believing he over-drove in the final segment of Qualifying.

"I think the lap was pretty good in Q3, it's a tricky Qualifying where you've got to go fully committed into Q3 and I did that," he said.

"But I felt like I maybe went over the limit a little in some corners and lost a little bit on top of maybe losing down the straights a bit because of running the older spec [engine].

"But at the end, that's on me. I think we did a good job today and we maximised our potential."

title: Dejected Oscar Piastri laments 'pretty shocking' qualifying effort
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri cut a frustrated figure following a "disappointing" grid-setting session at the Madring, which left him down in seventh whilst his McLaren team-mate Lando Norris nabbed pole.

Piastri struggled to keep his MCL40 in the groove, and it cost him, with his best time approaching five-tenths of a second slower than Norris in the sister car.

The Australian had fared better in qualifying of late, but will have considerable work to do during the Spanish Grand Prix to claw his way back up the order.

Reflecting on the session, the 25-year-old offered a blunt appraisal of his performance.

"The first lap wasn't too bad, but the second lap was pretty shocking. Disappointing," Piastri said to Sky Sports F1 after qualifying.

"Turn 1 didn't start well, and a few places were quite a bit better than the lap before, but once you get out of the rhythm, it makes the lap very tough."

Piastri 'wants' qualifying re-do

Heading into qualifying, Piastri had been relatively pleased with the performance of his McLaren, but was left wishing he could have a do-over.

"Not a great session," the nine-time grand prix winner added.

"The pace has been reasonable this weekend. It's just been about being there consistently.

"Unfortunately, one of those sessions you want again."

title: Liam Lawson puzzled by Red Bull regression: 'I don't really understand'
excerpt:
Liam Lawson was left confused by his Red Bull becoming increasingly uncompetitive during qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Lawson, who is still deputising for the injured Isack Hadjar in the RB22, could only go eighth-fastest in the grid-setting session at the Madring.

His final push lap was three-and-a-half tenths slower than Max Verstappen, who qualified third in the sister car.

Reflecting on his effort, Lawson contended that it could have been cleaner, but was predominantly concerned by his increasing lack of pace.

"Overall, through qualifying, we just somehow got less competitive than where we started," the 24-year-old told media, including RacingNews365. "Which, from where we were this morning, I don't really understand.

"It's something to review. With this car, it's obviously new to me what we do through qualifying.

"In my [usual] car, I know what we traditionally do with the front wing and things like that as the track evolves.

"But it's less clear to me in this car, and I think by Q3, we lost a little bit of the balance, and it wasn't the tidiest. So it's a shame, because I think we were very competitive before that."

Red Bull tyre management 'definitely got worse'

Like many of his peers, Lawson struggled to maintain tyre temperatures on the hot, punishing surface of the all-new circuit, with the long-radius banked La Monumental halfway through the lap putting considerable load through the rubber.

That left him unable to get the most out of the machinery at his disposal through the final part of the lap.

"Tyres for me, honestly, having them in the right window, especially through the lap," Lawson said when asked what the biggest challenge of qualifying was.

"For us, towards the end of the lap, I was struggling a lot in Sector 3.

"And it wasn't something we had earlier, so that definitely got worse. But I think outside of that, just balance this weekend and confidence in the car."

title: McLaren hails Lando Norris 'masterpiece' despite expensive mistake
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has branded Lando Norris' final push lap in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix a "masterpiece" after the F1 drivers' champion snatched pole position away from Kimi Antonelli.

The Briton was just 11 milliseconds quicker than the Mercedes driver at the Madring, but his boss revealed the 26-year-old lost three tenths of a second at the final corner, where Norris himself conceded he almost crashed.

However, he managed to hold onto his MCL40 by the ragged edge to claim his third pole position of the campaign (and his third in the past four rounds).

Norris' season has come alive since McLaren delivered upgrades for the Hungarian Grand Prix just before the summer break, and is — along with Antonelli — the in-form driver in F1.

He is undeniably brimming with confidence and was thrilled with his effort, the 19th pole of his career, telling his team it was "one of my best" over the radio.

Stella was inclined to agree, showering his driver in praise for his exploits at F1's newest circuit.

"It was a masterpiece," the Italian told Sky Sports F1. "We have seen across the whole weekend, if we put it all together, we are not far from the best cars.

"We worked our way step by step to try to put all the performance together. Lando did it only on the final run in Q3, and in the final corner he made a mistake of three tenths. It was an incredible lap - one of the best of his life until the last corner.

"He realised what was available in the car. We are happy with pole.

"At the same time, the grid is so tight that if you are a few tenths behind, like Oscar [Piastri, in the second McLaren], you are P7."

McLaren low-speed weakness alleviated after set-up evolution

McLaren has struggled in low-speed corners this season, but the team has continuously worked at refining its set-up to remedy the inherent weakness of its chassis.

With both Norris and Piastri having lacked confidence in the car early in the weekend, Stella was pleased to highlight the progress made in that area.

"In some of the previous races we talked about performance in the low-speed [corners]," the 55-year-old said.

"We saw the car was naturally fast in some of the high-speed, fast, flowing sections at the start of the weekend, but at low speed the drivers did not have confidence to brake and turn into the corners, so we evolved the setup and driving to give them more confidence - to the point we finished qualifying with the best first sector."

title: Lewis Hamilton suffers sudden Ferrari realisation as pole slips through fingers
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has described his sudden realisation that his Ferrari was set to struggle during the crunch point at the end of Spanish Grand Prix qualifying.

After the first runs in Q3, Hamilton held provisional pole and was on course for his first P1 start in a grand prix since the 2023 Hungarian GP, 73 races ago.

However, on the second run, Hamilton only improved his time by less than a tenth of a second, opening the door for rivals to leapfrog him.

Lando Norris, Kimi Antonelli, and Max Verstappen all broke the 1:32 barrier, by dipping into the 1:31s to leave Hamilton fourth on the grid - the second time this season he has lost out on pole in Q3 after leading the first runs, following Hungary, to Norris.

Reflecting, Hamilton was pleased with the performance his SF-26 had shown, but explained how he knew he was in trouble at the end of the out-lap of his second run.

"Qualifying was generally pretty straightforward, with no real issues," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"I felt pretty awesome on Q3 run one, and then just didn't have any more grip or power.

"It was good execution from the team. I think they did a really good job, but unfortunately, I just didn't have the pace [at the end]."

Later, speaking to Sky Sports F1, Hamilton expanded on some of the issues he faced during his second lap.

"The second lap was just as good as the other one, because it was the same time pretty much," he said.

"I think I was half a tenth quicker or something like that, but for some reason, we went into that last lap, and as I came around the last corner, I had understeer.

"I was like: 'Hey, maybe these front tyres are not switched on", and it just turns out that I had more rear and more understeer through the lap."

The article continues below.

Hamilton looks ahead to Spanish GP

As for the race itself, Hamilton was upbeat about the circuit, but wary of the lack of overtaking opportunities.

"I have no idea. I mean, I haven't seen the other races, but was told it was very hard to overtake," he said.

"It is a pretty cool track to drive, some go-kart-esque elements with the kerbs, which is cool, really cool banking, so I think they did a really great job."

title: Max Verstappen heavily criticises new Madring F1 circuit: 'That's BS'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has launched a pointed criticism of Formula 1's new Madring circuit, dismissing the idea that space constraints excuse the lack of overtaking opportunities as "BS".

Verstappen will start from third on the grid for Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix after finishing 0.140s adrift of pole-sitter in McLaren's Lando Norris, with championship leader Andrea Antonelli splitting the pair in second in his Mercedes.

Although the circuit presented a challenge for the drivers in qualifying, there are concerns the race will be a sterile one given the lack of passing places around the 22-corner layout.

Speaking to the media after qualifying, including RacingNews365, Verstappen said: "I like the grip. They did a good job with the Tarmac, even though in some places it's a bit too bumpy already for a new track.

"The corners, you can't overtake. So, in some places, the braking zones, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer, that you have to combine under braking, because it doesn't allow any kind of overtaking.

"For sure, in terms of track design, I think it can be better. I also think input from drivers in the future on track design can also help a lot.

"I know they will always come back to you and say, 'Yeah, but the space'. But that's BS. There's always a way to find an overtaking opportunity around a track."

Verstappen feels Madring changes needed for the future

Verstappen at least felt the event overall to be "very cool", and the organisers had done "a great job" in that respect.

He added: "Also, how quickly they made the track available, the information that was shared for the simulator, so in that sense, it's very good.

"But if you want to have better racing and overtaking, there are a few corners that can be changed."

Asked how Sunday's race is likely to unfold from his grid slot, the Red Bull driver replied: "It will be tough. Let's say, best-case scenario, you're faster, but you can't pass.

"There are no corners where you can pass, so you need to rely on people degging very aggressively, so it's going to be tough.

"The long runs here have been very tough, a lot of deg for everyone, so that will probably be the key point tomorrow, but even with that, I still need to figure out a corner where to pass."

title: George Russell recounts 'annoying' moment which wrecked Spanish GP qualifying
excerpt:
George Russell has detailed the "annoying" mistake which wrecked his Spanish Grand Prix qualifying and left him sixth on the grid.

Russell, who now trails team-mate Kimi Antonelli by 66 points in the drivers' standings, will be on the third row of the Madrid grid for the first grand prix in the Spanish capital since 1981, with Antonelli poised to extend his lead having taken second.

Russell did hold third place after the first runs in Q3 but was dumped down to sixth after Lando Norris improved to pole, with Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc also leapfrogging the Briton.

Recounting what had happened, Russell revealed how a time-loss at Turn 11, just before La Monumental, had ended his bid to earn a fifth pole of the season.

"No, I don't think so," Russell began to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if the wall tap had had any lasting damage.

"Obviously, it was slightly concerning in the moment, but the car was fine. I went out and topped the session afterwards, and then felt in the mix thereafter.

"But just the last lap, I was about three-tenths up, and at Turn 11, the tyres couldn't take it.

"I lost all the lap time thereafter, and so that was annoying.

"It is a strange [track surface]; it is very high-grip, but the tyres are sliding quite a lot, so [the race] is going to be really interesting with the [tyre] degradation."

The article continues below.

Russell bemoans lack of overtaking opportunities

On a track where overtaking looks difficult, Russell detailed how the design just did not aid overtaking, and pointed to the roundabout at Turns 5 and 6.

"It is Jeddah-esque because of the high-speed corners, but there is also some Baku with some awkward braking zones," he said.

"Maybe one small frustration is the design has a lack of clear overtaking opportunities. On every track, at the end of the long straight, you need a clear opportunity to overtake.

"And the longest straight here goes into a tight roundabout section."

title: Kimi Antonelli offers 'very intense' explanation after Lando Norris 'snatched away' pole
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli labelled qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix "very intense" after Lando Norris 'snatched away' pole position from the Mercedes driver.

The young Italian came up just 11 milliseconds short of the reigning F1 drivers' champion at the Madring.

It looked like Antonelli had done enough, but with Norris one of the last drivers to take the chequered flag, he was denied in gut-wrenching fashion.

Despite missing out on top spot, it was a good grid-setting session for Antonelli, with his nearest championship rivals, Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes team-mate George Russell, only able to go fourth and sixth-quickest, respectively.

Track position will be critical in the 57-lap race, with overtaking opportunities hard to come by on the all-new 22-corner circuit in the Spanish capital.

"I thought it was a good lap, but then this guy [gesturing to Norris] just snatched it away," Antonelli said after hopping out of his W17. "So good job to them [McLaren].

"On my side, a very intense qualifying. Difficult to get the balance right with the track being so hot, but the lap was pretty clean."

Antonelli details 'quite tricky' experience

Reflecting on how challenging the conditions were, Antonelli was keen to turn his focus to the grand prix, as he looks to extend his advantage over Russell from the current 66-point margin.

"Obviously, it's not easy to put the things together on a track like this, which is quite tricky," the seven-time grand prix winner added.

"But overall, I think we did a good job, and now we'll try to see what we can do tomorrow."

title: Lando Norris reveals crash fear ahead of nailing best lap of his F1 career
excerpt:
Lando Norris has revealed he came within inches of ploughing his McLaren into a wall en route to securing a sensational pole for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Norris did not appear in the mix before his stunning final lap at the new Madring circuit, but somehow finished just 0.011s ahead of championship leader Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli.

"I'm shocked," said Norris. "I'm a little bit surprised to be here now. My God, it was probably one of the best laps I've done - ever in my career."

Over the radio a few minutes earlier, Norris had said that his lap "might be the best one".

Declaring himself "very happy, very proud, very happy for the team", he added: "It was one of those laps where everything came together.

"I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, but it was whether my brain would let me do it on the last lap, and everything pretty much worked perfectly.

"I'm just very happy. It's one of those laps where you look at the lap time at the end, and you're like, 'Oh shit! That was pretty good'."

[Article continues below]

Norris feared overnight repairs for McLaren mechanics

The lap handed Norris the 19th pole of his F1 career, and third this season, but he confirmed it almost never was.

"The adrenaline was high on the last lap," he said. "It's just one where you have to relax, let it all flow. It's easy to get tense around here, and there are a lot of walls that come at you pretty quickly.

"Honestly, I've been feeling pretty confident, and the car was feeling good, so I felt pretty good out there. I just wasn't doing what I wanted. I wasn't feeling relaxed. The last lap, I just took a good breath, and everything came together.

"It was pretty much perfect, but the last corner I thought I was in the wall, and the boys would have to repair the car tonight.

"So it could have been a little bit better, but nevertheless, it was one of the best laps I've done. Everything I wanted to achieve, I achieved. That's one of the moments where you're in that flow state, and it has put a big smile on my face, so I'm happy."

title: Lando Norris stuns Kimi Antonelli to steal sizzling Spanish GP pole
excerpt:
Lando Norris denied Kimi Antonelli at the very end to steal the Spanish Grand Prix pole position as George Russell's challenge fell away.

Lando Norris stunned Kimi Antonelli at the end of Spanish Grand Prix qualifying to steal pole position by just 0.011s.

Norris, who missed all of FP2 with a gearbox issue, placed only sixth after the first runs in Q3, with Lewis Hamilton holding provisional pole ahead of Antonelli and George Russell.

However, on his final flying lap, Norris posted a 1:31.824 lap, just 0.011s faster than Antonelli, who had taken provisional pole from Hamilton.

Hamilton himself found only 0.066s on his second flying lap and slipped to fourth as Max Verstappen nipped ahead.

It is Norris's third pole of the season, with Charles Leclerc in fifth, and George Russell down in sixth, having been third after the first Q3 runs.

Lando Norris stuns Kimi Antonelli to steal sizzling Spanish GP pole

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Hamilton and then Norris on pole

After the first runs in Q3, Hamilton's 1:32.079s was good enough to hold provisional pole from Antonelli on a 1:32.140 and Norris on a 1:32.525 down in sixth place.

Antonelli initially then found 0.244s to move up to provisional pole as Russell's challenge faltered, leaving the door open for Norris.

He found 0.701s on his second lap, which he labelled as "one of the best laps" of his career.

It was 0.011s faster than Antonelli, with Verstappen in third, ahead of Hamilton in fourth, who found only less than a tenth of improvement on his second run.

Leclerc was fifth, ahead of Russell with Oscar Piastri, Liam Lawson, Franco Colapinto, and Arvid Lindblad rounding out the top 10.

© XPBimages

Gasly fails to equal Monza heroics

The big story in Q2 was the elimination of Italian GP pole-sitter Pierre Gasly.

Gasly, who like team-mate Colapinto had just a single run at the end of the segment, could only place 14th, nearly seven-tenths slower than Colapinto, who was eighth.

Nico Hulkenberg led the Audi's, but dropped out by 0.019s as Lindblad got through, with Gabriel Bortoleto slotting in behind his team-mate.

Esteban Ocon was 13th ahead of Gasly in 14th, with Yuki Tsunoda and Alex Albon completing the eliminees in 15th and 16th.

Up front, Verstappen topped the segment from Antonelli and Hamilton.

© XPBimages

Double Spanish disappointment in Q1 in Madrid

Following his FP3 accident earlier in the day, Oliver Bearman was ruled out of qualifying, meaning just five cars were eliminated in Q1.

It was a double Spanish disappointment following the segment, as Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso were both eliminated.

Sainz fell just 0.005s from safety, dropping team-mate Albon into the drop-zone.

Both Cadillacs also fell, with Sergio Perez out-qualifying Valtteri Bottas once again, as Bearman and Lance Stroll failed to set a lap-time.

Stroll was set to start at the rear regardless, owing to power unit component changes.

Up front, Russell topped the segment from Antonelli and Lawson, as Verstappen, Hamilton, and Leclerc all got through by using the medium tyres.
